guidance:
Use only Table 1 to define structure and values. Do not import data from narrative text or footnotes; use them only to clarify layout.

1) Overall scope
- Set `table_title` from the caption of Table 1.
- Work strictly inside the visible bounds of Table 1.

2) Columns and headers
- Reconstruct the entire header region (all header rows) from left to right before creating any cells.
- Add every explicit data column header to `columns`: each group/arm, timepoint, and any separate statistics column (such as risk measures, p values, standardized differences, etc.).
- For multi-row or nested headers where a top header spans subheaders, treat only the lowest-level headers as data columns. Form each `column_label` by concatenating the higher-level text and the leaf header (e.g., "Top: Leaf"), and include that combined text once in `columns`.
- Do not treat a purely grouping header as a separate column.
- If the leftmost label column has its own heading, include that heading string in `columns`, but never create data cells for that column; its contents become `row_group` and `row_label`.
- Every `column_label` used in any cell must appear exactly once in `columns`. Do not invent additional columns (totals, combined groups) unless they are printed as header cells.

3) Row structure: separating groups from labels
- Use the first column to distinguish structure from data:
  • Section or category headings: visually distinct, often spanning multiple columns or followed by several related rows.
  • Data rows: aligned with entries in one or more data columns.
- Treat each section or category heading as a `row_group`. All subsequent data rows clearly under that heading use that text verbatim as `row_group`, and their own leftmost cell text as `row_label`.
- Rows that are not obviously under any heading use `row_group` = null.
- If a section heading itself has data values on the same line, represent that line with `row_group` equal to the heading text and `row_label` = null.
- Do not swap roles: `row_group` is always the broader section; `row_label` is the specific item. Do not move section text into `row_label` or item text into `row_group`.
- When the same heading or item appears multiple times, reuse the exact wording so that grouping remains consistent.

4) Cells and values
- A cell corresponds to one non-empty intersection of a data row and a data column.
- For every visible numeric or textual entry in the body of Table 1, create exactly one cell object with `row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`, and `value`.
- Copy `value` verbatim, including digits, punctuation, spaces, parentheses, ranges, units, percent signs, plus/minus signs, and textual markers such as N/A-like terms or dashes when they appear as values.
- Printed zeros are real values and must be included.
- Do not emit cells for blank table entries. Never infer, calculate, or move values between rows or columns.

5) Avoid missing, extra, and duplicate cells
- Work row by row. For each data row, scan across all data columns and add one cell for every non-empty entry; do not add cells where the table cell is blank.
- Do not create cells for rows that are purely headers or section titles with no data values.
- Do not add derived totals, combined values, or subgroup cells unless they appear explicitly as table entries.
- Each combination of (`row_group`, `row_label`, `column_label`) must be unique; never emit more than one cell for the same position.

6) String consistency
- Use table wording verbatim for `table_title`, `columns`, `row_group`, `row_label`, and `column_label`, preserving spelling, capitalization, spacing, and symbols.
- Ensure that every `column_label` in `cells` exactly matches one entry in `columns`, and that repeated section headings used as `row_group` are written identically wherever they occur.

Apply these rules consistently to capture the full structure of Table 1 and every non-empty value in its correct row and column without adding, omitting, or rearranging data.
